To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the security of some countermeasures against malicious fault attacks has been overrated in the literature, and that, in general, the security/efficiency of countermeasures can be improved through design improvements."

the countermeasures proposed in the literature do not always provide better security than the naive solutions and that the security of many countermeasures depends on unrealistic assumptions (e.g. about the fault model, the attacker's knowledge, etc.)

the most efficient protection is a simple repetition (e.g., 3 times), that the best security/efficiency ratio is obtained by using a combination of repetition and error detection/corrections, and that the best security is obtained with a combination of repetition, error detection/correcton and masking (the latter is the most expensive solution).
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: What are the security and cost implications of various countermeasures against fault attacks?
the design of efficient fault-tolerant cryptographic systems.
the following question: how to efficiently and securely protect cryptographic devices against fault attacks?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, while some recent countermeasures have shown promising security, the majority of existing solutions are not better than naive solutions, and that there is still much room for improvements in the design of fault attack countermeasures.
, in general, the cost of protection is high and the security is low.
, while some of the countermeasure techniques are very effective against fault attacks, others are not, and still others can be improved.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, although some of the countermeasure techniques are promising, the security and performance of most countermeasure solutions is still far from satisfactory.
the security of a countermeasure is only as good as the weakest link in its design.
, in general, fault attacks are not a serious threat to AES implementations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in the context of fault attacks, the choice of a countermeasure is not as straightforward as one would expect.

, for the time being, the most secure and efficient solution to protect against fault attacks is to use a combination of duplication and repetition, with the former providing the best protection against random faults, and the latter being most effective against malicious faults.

, for any given security requirement, the best protection against fault attacks is not necessarily the one that is the most complex, but the one that is most efficient in terms of security/cost tradeoff.
